Despite its current energy challenges, Africa has

content.title: Vast renewable energy potential and a rich reserve of critical minerals (like cobalt, lithium, and rare earth elements) that are vital to the global clean energy transition.
A strategic opportunity to leapfrog to modern, green energy systems, closing the electricity and clean cooking access gaps that affect over 900 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa.

content.text: This lesson discusses the African context by exploring Africa’s energy and economic situation. Furthermore, it highlights the development focus for the region, having discussed its particular challenges.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: A: Development Context in Africa

content.text: 80% of people without electricity in sub-Saharan Africa live in rural areas

Africa’s rural-urban divide presents a major challenge to sustainable development, particularly in the energy sector. While urban areas increasingly benefit from grid connectivity and infrastructure investments, rural communities remain disproportionately underserved—over 80% of people without electricity in sub-Saharan Africa live in rural areas. This imbalance, also seen in the measure of clean energy equity index across the region, hinders poverty reduction, limits access to education and healthcare, and exacerbates migration pressures toward cities. Addressing this divide is critical for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 7 on affordable and clean energy.
By 2050, Africa is projected to account for 25% of the world’s population.

Africa is poised to become a central player in global <ai prompt="What is energy markets?">energy markets 💬️</ai>, projected to account for 25% of the world’s population by 2050, with rising urbanization, middle-class consumption, and growing demand for clean energy.

content.title: Africa offers some of the highest returns on renewable energy investments globally (IRENA, 2022)
content.body: With strong governance and climate finance, Africa is not just a future energy market—it is the frontier of energy growth.

content.title: Over 60% of Africa’s population is under 25
content.body: Yet youth unemployment remains high and technical skills are lacking. Addressing this skills gap through vocational training, technical education, and green innovation hubs will be essential to enable youth and marginalized groups to fully participate in and benefit from the renewable energy transition.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: B: Energy Challenges in Africa

content.text: Across the globe, energy poverty remains a persistent barrier to development, with 666 million people still lacking access to electricity and 2.1 billion without access to <ai prompt="What is clean cooking?">clean cooking 💬️</ai> solutions. Nowhere is this challenge more acute - and more urgent - than in Sub-Saharan Africa.
In this region alone, 565 million people live without electricity, representing 83% of the global electricity access deficit.

Countries like Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Ethiopia are home to nearly one-third of the world’s population without electricity. This isn't just a statistic, it reflects hundreds of millions of people whose daily lives, economic potential, and health are compromised due to the absence of reliable energy.

content.title: Access to clean cooking in Sub-Saharan Africa is a critical and urgent issue.
content.description: Approximately 923 million people—nearly half of the global population lacking clean cooking—still depend on wood, charcoal, or other biomass fuels. These are typically burned in open fires or traditional stoves, leading to severe health risks from indoor air pollution, especially for women and girls who also spend long hours collecting fuel. Addressing this challenge can yield multiple benefits: better health outcomes, enhanced gender equality, and reduced environmental degradation. Achieving universal energy access in Africa could also boost GDP growth by up to 6% annually in some countries (World Bank, 2022).

content.text: Africa’s economy remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels with 12 countries holding proven oil reserves—Libya, Nigeria, and Angola alone account for about 5% of global reserves.

content.body: In these nations, oil and gas make up over 85% of export earnings, leaving their economies vulnerable to global market fluctuations. Despite this wealth, human development remains low in many fossil fuel-rich countries, such as Chad (HDI 0.394), Republic of Congo (0.479), Nigeria (0.535), and Tanzania (0.549).

Notably, 62% of the world’s poor now live in Sub-Saharan Africa’s resource-rich economies, a sharp rise from 13% in 2000, highlighting that fossil fuel dependence has not led to inclusive or sustained development. Although recent geopolitical events, like the energy crisis from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, have temporarily boosted African gas demand, this is not a long-term fix.

Additionally, fossil fuel extraction in Africa is 15-20% more costly and 70-80% more carbon-intensive than elsewhere, increasing risks of stranded assets as global fossil fuel demand falls and debts rise.

content.text: Amid these challenges lies a significant opportunity: investing in renewables such as solar, wind, mini-grids, and clean cooking technologies can bridge energy access gaps while fostering economic diversification, stability, and inclusion. Renewable infrastructure supports supply chains and skilled labor, enabling job creation and new markets, especially in underserved rural and peri-urban communities through local solar and off-grid providers.

content.text: Except for cobalt – where the DRC accounts for approximately 70% of global production – Africa's contribution to global production remains relatively small.
With responsible mining practices, Africa can actively participate in the development of value-added products during the energy transition

Processing operations are primarily concentrated in China, accounting for 35% of nickel, 50-70% of lithium, and cobalt, and 90% of rare earth elements. For instance, Zimbabwe, the sixth-largest global lithium producer, could potentially supply up to 20% of the global lithium market, but currently only accounts for 1% of global lithium supply.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: C: Energy Opportunities in Africa

content.text: Africa’s renewable abundance makes it one of the most competitive regions for green hydrogen production

content.title: Countries like Namibia, Mauritania, Egypt, and South Africa are developing large-scale hydrogen projects.
content.body: Green hydrogen can power industries, replace imported fertilizers, and serve as a clean fuel for export, particularly to Europe.

content.title: Africa could produce up to 5,000 megatonnes of hydrogen per year at less than $2/kg by 2050 - equal to the world’s current energy supply (IEA, 2023).
content.body: This could position Africa as a global supplier of sustainable fuels, creating high-tech industries and boosting export revenues.

content.text: Africa’s role in the global economy could be redefined

content.title: 76% of Africa’s electricity generation could be renewable by 2040, if the right investments and policy frameworks are adopted (IRENA, 2021).

Africa holds 30% of the world’s essential minerals required for renewable technologies such as lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements - critical for batteries, wind turbines, and solar panels (IEA, 2023).
The continent also possesses 60% of the world’s best solar resources, making it uniquely positioned to become a global renewable energy leader (IRENA, 2022).

content.text: This clean energy potential could redefine Africa’s role in the global economy - transforming it from an exporter of raw resources into a hub of green industrialization, innovation, and resilience.
Africa need more installed electricity capacity

Currently, Africa’s installed electricity capacity stands at 369 gigawatts (GW)—only 16% of China’s capacity. The average per capita electricity consumption in Sub-Saharan Africa is a mere 200 kWh per year, barely enough to power a few lightbulbs and a small fan. For comparison, China’s consumption is 4,500 kWh, India’s is 1,300 kWh, and Brazil’s is 2,360 kWh. Experts estimate that at least 1,000 kWh per person per year is needed to sustain a path of productive economic development.


Although progress has been made over the past decades, much more needs to be done, especially to obtain a normal and not skewed distribution between the states in the region - South Africa and Egypt alone account for nearly 50% of total electricity production in the region. Off-Grid and Decentralized Power are game changers

With over 80% of Africa’s unelectrified population in rural areas, off-grid solar, mini-grids, and battery storage systems are game changers.

Companies like M-KOPA and d.light are already reaching millions of households with pay-as-you-go solar kits.
decentralized energy systems 💬️ can bypass the cost and time of grid extension, offering faster, cleaner access to power.

These solutions create opportunities for local entrepreneurship, digital payments, and financial inclusion..
Financial investment is critical
To achieve universal energy access by 2030, Africa must secure $25 billion in annual investments
Yet, between 2000 and 2020, the continent attracted just 2% of the $2.8 trillion invested globally in renewables, highlighting a significant financing gap.

Scaling up energy finance is not only essential for climate goals but is also a development priority, especially as fossil-fuel-dependent economies face increasing risks. Renewable energy offers Africa a chance to diversify economically, foster resilience, and transition to a digital, climate-smart economy.
African Union Agenda
The AU’s Agenda 2063 already sets an ambitious aspiration to realize

content.quote: “a prosperous Africa based on inclusive growth and sustainable development”.

content.text: This vision is rooted in the need to deliver energy security through interconnected infrastructure and a shift towards “modern, efficient, reliable, cost-effective, renewable and environmentally friendly” energy systems.
Industrial and Supply Chain Development
Africa’s mineral wealth, if harnessed responsibly, can form the backbone of local and regional manufacturing:

content.title: Countries like the DRC (70% of global cobalt) and Zimbabwe (significant lithium reserves) can establish local processing and battery manufacturing industries.
Regional supply chains can be developed for solar panels, wind turbines, batteries, and electric vehicles, fueling local economies and reducing import dependency.

content.text: This would move Africa up the value chain, away from raw exports and towards job-rich, high-value production, attracting foreign direct investment.
Regional cooperation can make energy solutions more cost effective.

Initiatives such as the West African Power Pool, which cover 14 out of 15 countries in the region’s economic block, attempts to integrate national power systems into a unified regional electricity market.
Development of the Lobito Corridor, spanning DRC, Angola, and Zambia, can strengthen regional supply chains related to batteries

takeaways.title: Africa’s Energy Landscape Faces Deep Challenges but Offers Immense Potential. The continent has significant renewable energy potential and critical minerals needed for clean energy technologies, positioning it as a key player in the global energy transition.

The Economic Reality Underscores the Need for a Just Transition Only 2% of global renewable energy investments between 2000–2020 went to Africa — highlighting the need for massive, targeted financing.

UNDP’s Regional Strategy Provides a Framework for Equitable Energy Transformation It promotes six enabling activities, including energy finance, digitalization, effective governance, innovation, skills training, and gender mainstreaming.
